message: Root-cause the 200-call crash end to end: the CRT heap handle is never initialised
note: Full chain, each link probed not assumed. (1) 0x005D9C04 is the CRT heap handle. Byte-scanned all of .text for every direct-write encoding (A3/89 /r/C7 05): the address appears exactly 4 times and all four are reads - push, cmp, cmp, cmp. Ghidra agrees: 4 refs, 0 writes. Nothing in the binary ever initialises it. (2) sub_003437F3 - which Ghidra's FidDb names _malloc - passes that NULL handle to the real allocator, so allocation fails and returns 0. (3) sub_00236500 does 'if (eax==0) eax=0' and stores it, so the default allocator global 0x5BBAB4 becomes NULL. Probe: '[ALLOCVAL] setting default allocator = 00000000'. (4) sub_002235D0 reads index 0x5BC544 = 0, which takes the FALLBACK branch to 0x5BBAB4, not the table. Probe: '[REGREAD] idx=0 default=00000000'. (5) It dereferences NULL -> crash. CORRECTION to the previous entry: the 0x5BB700 table being empty is a symptom, not the cause - sub_00216210 (the register function) is never called at all (0 hits), so the index stays 0 and the table is never consulted. Fix belongs in the port's XAPI/CRT startup, which already overrides sub_001A1C23; it must create a heap and store the handle at 0x5D9C04 before game code runs.

message: Correct the heap diagnosis: handle IS valid; failure is inside the lifted RtlAllocateHeap
note: TWO CORRECTIONS to the previous entry, both from probing. (1) 0x5D9C04 is NOT a heap handle - it is _newmode, the MSVC CRT 'call the new-handler on failure' flag. sub_003437C7 reads it only as 'if (arg2 == 0) give up', so 0 is a legitimate default and its never-being-written is not a bug. (2) The real handle is 0x5DD0E8, and it IS written, by sub_001A23F3 = _heap_init, which calls RtlCreateHeap with the reserve/commit from the XBE header at 0x10134/0x10138. Probed: it returns valid handles (00F81000, 01081000, 01181000, 01281000 - note it runs FOUR times, each creating a new heap and overwriting the previous, which leaks but is not the crash). GetProcessHeap (sub_0019ED75, a 6-byte 'mov eax,[0x5DD0E8]; ret') returns a valid handle at every use. So the chain is: valid handle -> HeapAlloc(handle, 0, 0x1A84) still returns 0 -> default allocator NULL -> registrar derefs NULL -> crash. The failure is INSIDE sub_001A0B0C, the lifted RtlAllocateHeap, which is SEH-wrapped. Also tested: applying the __SEH_epilog fix on top of the current build is much WORSE (200 -> 50 calls, heap 49 -> 2); reverted per Rule #14. message: Find the 49x _heap_init: XAPI process startup re-enters itself 71 times
note: sub_001A23F3 has NO direct callers in generated code - it is called once from sub_001A1C23, the XAPI process-startup override in recomp_manual.c. message: Fix TLS: XBE TLS directory was never processed - 339K -> 47.6M indirect calls
note: Crash was sub_00346743+0x130 reading 0xFFFFFF6C. Two real bugs, both confirmed against ground truth. (1) fs:[4] is the TLS slot array on Xbox, NOT the NT_TIB StackBase. xbox_memory_layout.c set it to XBOX_STACK_TOP on the Win32 assumption; all NINE MEM32(4) sites in the lifted code are the same pattern - idx=MEM32(0x5BA794); block=MEM32(fs4 + idx*4); block[+8]/[+0xC] - and not one treats it as a stack address. Now points at a real 16-slot array. (2) __tls_index held -37, so the lookup indexed 148 bytes BELOW the array. The XBE's TLS directory names tls_index_addr = 0x005BA794, which matches the read address and Ghidra's XAPILIB___tls_index exactly - the port never processed that directory, so the loader-assigned slot was never written. Set it to 0 in the XAPI startup override. Result: crash GONE (2/2 clean), total indirect calls 339,033 -> 47,621,890 (140x more code executing). kernel_calls flat at 200 - the proxy is blind again. New failure mode: 234 failed icalls on sequential small integers (0x0,0x1,0x2,...), the index-table-as-function-pointer pattern, now surfacing at far greater depth. Context: the lifter drops fs: prefixes entirely - 2,660 sites, mostly MEM32(0) for fs:[0] SEH - and the fake TIB at VA 0 is the workaround.

message: Save-area fix retried a third time and rejected: it is superseded, not mis-sequenced
note: Applied the [ebp-24] __SEH_epilog fix again now that the frame is published: 200 -> 52 kernel calls, heap 49 -> 2. Third rejection (40, 50, 52 against a 200 baseline). Reverted. Verified the premise against __SEH_prolog rather than trusting the comment - it really does 'MEM32(ebp-24) = esp' immediately after pushing ebx, esi, edi, so [save+0]=edi, [save+4]=esi, [save+8]=ebx and [save-4]=return address are all CORRECT offsets. The fix is not wrong about the layout; it is solving a problem that no longer exists. It was a workaround for esp drift, and the fall-through-edge fix plus the g_seh_ebp sync removed the drift at source. With esp no longer drifting the original POP32s read the right slots, and the save-area read now INTRODUCES error rather than avoiding it. Conclusion: retire it. Keep the drift fixed at source instead of compensating downstream.

message: Heap-range guards tested and KEPT: still load-bearing, unlike the save-area fix
note: Hypothesis: since the __SEH_epilog save-area workaround became actively harmful once esp drift was fixed at source, the other drift-era guards might have too. Five edits in the store cite stack escape/drift as their reason; 14 heap-range 'this' guards exist in gen. Disabled all 14 (condition made unreachable, exactly reversible) and measured: 200 -> 44 kernel calls, heap 49 -> 2. Re-enabled. So the hypothesis is WRONG - these guards still earn their place, and 'workarounds outlive their causes' does not generalise from one case. The pointers they reject are still genuinely bad, which means there is remaining corruption they are absorbing; that is worth finding, but they must not be removed first. Also hit CLAUDE.md trap #1 on the way (built a C string literal through a shell heredoc, the \n arrived as a real newline and broke the build) - should have used add_probe.py.

message: Restored: 200 kernel calls, guards re-enabled, tree clean
Guard instrumentation: only 2 of 14 guards are live, both in SEH exception dispatch
note: Probed all 9 distinct guard sites with add_probe.py. SEVEN NEVER EXECUTE (sub_00123600, sub_001F75A3, sub_00202CC0, sub_0020E520 x2, sub_0020E547, sub_002155B0) - they sit on paths the boot no longer takes, so they are dead weight, not protection. Only two fire on the live path, and both are SEH internals: sub_003432FC is _except_handler3 (Ghidra signature (ExceptionRecord, EstablisherFrame, Context), tests *(param_1+4) & 6 for EXCEPTION_UNWINDING, and __SEH_prolog pushes 0x3432FC as exactly that handler), and sub_003433B1 is the unwinder it calls. Entered 3 times each. G9 fires with ebx=0 - a NULL establisher/context frame handed to the unwinder. So the thing 'corrupting pointers' is not random memory damage: SEH exception dispatch is running during __cinit and unwinding with a null frame. That also explains why disabling the guards cost 200 -> 44: the two live ones are absorbing a real null, not a phantom. Next: find what raises the exception - a faulting constructor, or normal scope-exit unwind the port mis-models.

message: SEH during __cinit is NORMAL scope-exit unwinding, not a fault
note: Traced it: no exception is being raised at all. RtlRaiseException called 0 times (the bridge logs every call), VEH caught 0 host faults, and RtlUnwind (ordinal 292) is not among the 15 ordinals used. _except_handler3 (sub_003432FC) has ZERO direct callers - it is only ever pushed as a handler address (6 sites) and entered indirectly. The caller is sub_0034139A, which Ghidra's FidDb identifies outright as __local_unwind2, 'Library Function - Single Match, Visual Studio 2003 Release'. That is MSVC try/finally SCOPE-EXIT unwinding: __cinit wraps constructors in try/finally so a throwing ctor unwinds cleanly, and __local_unwind2 runs on normal exit too. So SEH machinery running during __cinit is correct CRT behaviour, not evidence of a fault - I was hunting an exception that does not exist. Follow-on: the ebx=0 that sub_003433B1's guard rejects is very likely a LEGITIMATE null ContextRecord, which is normal during unwind (context is not needed). If so that guard skips work on correct input. It cannot simply be deleted though - disabling the guards cost 200 -> 44 - so the dependency needs isolating rather than assuming.

message: Guard dependency isolated: 1 of 14 is load-bearing, and it masks a null EstablisherFrame
note: Disabling ONLY sub_003433B1's guard reproduces the whole regression - 200 -> 44 kernel calls, heap 49 -> 2, identical to disabling all fourteen. So exactly one guard is load-bearing and the other thirteen are inert (seven of those never execute at all). What it protects: 'if (!(ebx in heap range)) { eax = 1; return; }' sits immediately before 'ebp = ebx + 0x10', which derives a FRAME POINTER from ebx. record+0x10 is the classic _except_handler3 frame-base derivation, so ebx is the EstablisherFrame, not the Context as the guard comment says - and it is NULL. Without the guard ebp becomes 0x10 and everything downstream runs on a bogus frame; measured, that spins with ~9,000 safe-stub hits (and was the first NON-DETERMINISTIC result smoke_spread has flagged, 9079 vs 9088). CORRECTION to the previous entry: I guessed ebx=0 was a legitimate null ContextRecord and that the guard was skipping work on correct input. Wrong - an EstablisherFrame is never legitimately null. The guard is correct and necessary; it is masking a real defect upstream. Next: _except_handler3 is entered with a null EstablisherFrame, and that value comes off the SEH chain at fs:[0] - which the port fakes at VA 0 as a single global head, with no per-thread separation.

message: Null EstablisherFrame traced to a corrupt SEH chain head - NOT fixed, needs a design change
note: Probed _except_handler3's actual arguments. Two patterns alternate: (a) ExcRec=0 EstFrame=0 Ctx=001A1C23 Disp=0 - Ctx holding a FUNCTION ADDRESS (sub_001A1C23, the XAPI startup) means these are not SEH arguments at all, just stack garbage; (b) ExcRec=FFFFFFFF EstFrame=00F7FF98 - the end-of-chain marker arriving as an ExceptionRecord. In every case chainhead (fs:[0], i.e. MEM32(0)) reads 0x000000FF. xbox_memory_layout.c initialises it to 0xFFFFFFFF, so a DWORD write put 0xFF there - and the only writer on that path is __SEH_epilog's 'MEM32(0) = ecx' with ecx = MEM32(ebp-16), i.e. a corrupt frame. That is circular: corrupt frame -> corrupt chain -> corrupt frame. Ruled out: the single MEM8(0) site is in sub_00067DF0 which is never reached, and a byte write of 0xFF over 0xFFFFFFFF would leave 0xFFFFFFFF anyway. DELIBERATELY NOT PATCHED. The guard at sub_003433B1 already contains the damage and is worth 156 kernel calls; a speculative fix on top of a self-reinforcing corruption would most likely just move it. The real issue is structural: 63 SEH prologs and 58 epilogs all share ONE chain head, because the lifter drops fs: prefixes (2,660 sites) and the port fakes a single global TIB at VA 0. Correct fix is per-context SEH state, not another guard.

message: SEH chain head is ALREADY corrupt before any SEH runs - narrows the scope
note: Probed the very first __SEH_prolog: it reads chainhead = 0x000000FF, not the 0xFFFFFFFF that xbox_memory_layout.c writes (the TIB init log confirms it ran). And at the first __SEH_epilog, ebp is a perfectly valid stack address (00F7FF2C) with [ebp-16] already holding 0xFF. So the corruption is NOT produced by the unwinding machinery - VA 0 is already wrong before the first SEH prolog executes. That invalidates Option A in docs/SEH_SCOPE.md, which assumed the epilog wrote bad values from a bad frame; the epilog is faithfully saving and restoring a value that was already corrupt. Also corrects an earlier claim: I said the single MEM8(0) site (sub_00067DF0) was never reached, based on grepping stderr for the function name - but function names are not logged, so that check was meaningless. Probed it properly: 0 hits, it genuinely never runs. Remaining question is narrow and well-posed: what changes VA 0 from 0xFFFFFFFF to 0x000000FF between xbox_memory_layout init and the first SEH prolog? 0x000000FF is 0xFFFFFFFF with the top three bytes zeroed, or a dword write of 0xFF.

message: ROOT CAUSE: ordinal 47 was wired to the wrong handler and wrote through a BOOLEAN
note: Built a TIB write-watch in main.c (VirtualProtect the VA-0 page read-only after init; the VEH names the first writer, then self-disarms). It caught the corruption exactly: chain head was 0xFFFFFFFF at arm time, and the first write was to Xbox VA 0x00000001 from the kernel bridge - a zero dword at VA 1 turns bytes FF FF FF FF into FF 00 00 00, which reads as 0x000000FF. Exact match for the value seen. Cause: the bridge handler table mapped ordinal 47 to bridge_HalReadSMCTrayState, which treats arg1 as an OUTPUT POINTER. Ordinal 47 is actually HalRegisterShutdownNotification(Registration, Register) - kernel_thunks.c had the right name all along, only the bridge table disagreed - and its arg1 is the BOOLEAN 1. So 'if (count_ptr) BRIDGE_MEM32(count_ptr) = 0;' wrote through the address 1. The game's own call site (push ebx=1; push 0x461694) was already documented in a comment two hundred lines away. Fixed: added bridge_HalRegisterShutdownNotification (writes nothing), moved HalReadSMCTrayState to its real ordinal 46 (previously unmapped), and added BRIDGE_PTR_OK - 'if (ptr)' only rejects 0, so flags passed as pointers sailed through it. Verified: first TIB write is now sub_003432A8 (__SEH_prolog) at VA 0, legitimately installing the chain, and zero corrupt-chainhead reports. Kernel calls 200 -> 82 - Rule #1's two-different-programs case, the boot now takes a correct path and stops elsewhere: sub_0034139A+0x1BA (__local_unwind2) reading 0xF42BFFE0.

message: Mechanism at 82 calls fully mapped: _except_handler3 gets a non-record as its EstablisherFrame
note: Probed the very first __local_unwind2 call: rec=00F7FF98 handler=00000000 scopetab=00F7FFD4 trylevel=00000000. A real SEH registration record is {prev, handler, scopetable, trylevel} - handler is never 0 and scopetable is a .data pointer like 0x430838, not a stack address. So the EstablisherFrame handed to _except_handler3 is not a registration record, just arbitrary stack memory. __local_unwind2 then does exactly what it is written to do: reads trylevel 0, passes the !=-1 and !=param_2 checks, reads scopetable[0].previousTryLevel from stack garbage, WRITES THAT BACK into the record's trylevel field, calls scopetable[0].handler (also garbage), and on the next iteration reads the corrupted trylevel 0x3CCD0003, multiplies by 3 and faults. It destroys its own loop variable on the first pass. Also self-feeding: those bogus handler calls are mostly rejected by the plausibility filter as stack addresses, but one lands on 0x3432FC and re-enters _except_handler3. Confirmed via the icall ring buffer at handler entry: targets were 003432FC, 00F7FF10, 00F7FF0C - consecutive stack slots. sub_003433B1 is a FRAGMENT of _except_handler3 (181 bytes in), and its guard admits [0x880000,0x4000000), a range the stack falls inside, so it cannot reject a stack address that is not a record. Remaining question: what invokes _except_handler3 with a non-record, given nothing raises an exception (0 RtlRaiseException, 0 VEH, no RtlUnwind) - the call arrives from inside __cinit.

message: Global x87 stack: the FPU is a machine resource, not per-frame
note: The lifter emitted 'double _fp_stack[8]; int _fp_top = 0;' as FUNCTION LOCALS. On x86 the x87 stack is global state - a function returning float or double leaves the value in st(0) and the caller pops it with fstp. With a per-frame stack every such return value was destroyed at the call boundary and the caller popped an uninitialised slot. Exactly the ebp/g_seh_ebp bug class. Fixed in translator.py (macros now alias g_fp_stack/g_fp_top, defined in xbox_memory_layout.c) and applied to the existing gen/ by tools_data/apply_global_fpstack.py, which emits byte-identical lines so the pending regeneration is a no-op for them. Also added fp_st(n) for the register forms Stage B needs. Signals unchanged at 82/4/3/8 with an identical crash site over 2 runs - expected, since the boot dies in __local_unwind2 long before float returns matter. Recorded as a correctness fix with no boot signal, not as progress.

message: x87 and MMX implemented: 9,099 dropped instructions -> 182, plus 16,147 silent stack-depth fixes
note: Measured the real gap first instead of trusting the earlier '550 missing instructions' estimate, which was counted wrong twice - once too low (my grep only saw the '/* mnemonic' form and missed the 623 MMX sites emitted as '/* TODO:'), once too high in kind (the biggest hole was never SIMD at all, it was x87). THE DROPPED SET: fnstsw 3556, fstp 1927, fld 1435, fcos 448, movq 272, fdivr 236, fsubr 201, paddw 152, psraw 88, packuswb 87, pextrw 84, fsin 60, psrlq 37, paddusw 32, punpcklbw 30, pmullw 24 and a long tail - 9,099 instructions that emitted a bare C comment. Now 182, and 172 of those are correct: 90 are 3DNow! (pfmul/pfadd), unreachable because recomp_cpuid reports an Intel Pentium III and the game dispatches on AMD extended bits; 18 emms/femms, which are no-ops here because MMX is modelled independently of x87 rather than aliased onto it; 6 prefetch hints; 2 fnclex. The genuine remainder is 62 packed-float sites (shufps 56, unpcklps/unpckhps/movhlps 2 each) - see below. THE SILENT-WRONG SET, which no drop count showed and no build error could catch: the x87 model had the stack DEPTH wrong in four places, and depth errors cascade because every st(n) is relative to TOP. fst popped when it must not (627 sites), fcomp/fcompp/fucompp never popped when they must (3,146), and fadd/fsub/fmul/fdiv popped unconditionally even for a memory operand, which never pops (12,374). 16,147 sites total, now verified correct: every non-p arithmetic form emits no pop and every p-form does. ARCHITECTURAL: _fp_stack/_fp_top were FUNCTION LOCALS. The x87 stack is a machine resource - a function returning float or double leaves it in st(0) for the caller to pop - so every float return value was destroyed at the call boundary. Same bug class as ebp, same fix as g_seh_ebp: they are now g_fp_stack/g_fp_top. VERIFICATION: tools/recomp/test_fpu.py checks mnemonic decomposition and per-form stack depth (37 cases); tools_data/test_mmx_helpers.c compiles standalone and checks 30 lane-order, saturation and packing boundaries - it caught one bad expectation of mine, not a bad helper. Signals unchanged at 82/4/3/8, deterministic over 2 runs, identical crash site: the boot still dies in __local_unwind2 long before this code runs, so this is recorded as correctness with no boot signal, NOT as progress. NEXT: xmm is modelled as a single C float, but it is 128 bits - four lanes. That is why shufps and the packed-float ops still emit comments, and it means movaps only copies a quarter of the register. Contained job, same class as this one.

message: ROOT CAUSE: an unresolved stub never purged its args, destroying _initterm's table cursor
note: The boot died in __local_unwind2 with an EstablisherFrame that was not a registration record, in a run where nothing ever raised an exception. Chain, measured not inferred: _initterm (sub_001A3554) walks the CRT initialiser table with the cursor in esi; after calling entry 0x44A598 the cursor came back as 0x00F7FF0C, a STACK address, so the loop left the table and called every dword it found - one of which was _except_handler3, which is how the SEH unwinder was entered with garbage. Traced down: _initterm -> sub_003556E0 -> sub_00340DE6 -> sub_00340DAE -> sub_00340D06 -> sub_00345ACC, where esp was measured drifting 0x10 across the call to sub_001A016A, so __SEH_epilog restored ebx/esi/edi from 16 bytes off-target. The drift came from sub_001A0189, which was an EMPTY STUB in recomp_stubs_unresolved.c ('not detected'). The real code is 5 instructions ending in 'ret 0xc'. In this calling convention the callee pops the fake return address, so a do-nothing stub pops NOTHING and leaks 16 bytes of simulated stack per call. Fixed by seeding it (seed_missing_functions.py --va 0x001A0189). THIS IS A CLASS, NOT A ONE-OFF: there are 3,205 unresolved stubs and every one of them is a silent stack leak whenever it is called. RESULT: kernel calls 82 -> 52, but that count is the wrong lens (Rule #8) - failed indirect calls 4 -> 1 and safe-stub hits 8 -> 1, because the stack-walking garbage loop is gone entirely. The boot now reaches GAME code (sub_002235D0/sub_002221E0/sub_00209650 at 0x22xxxx) instead of dying in the CRT at 0x34xxxx. New blocker is the same class: esp has gone NEGATIVE (0xFFFFFF44). TOOLS BUILT: recomp_where() + add_probe --where + triage --where (probe-callable native backtrace); RECOMP_CHECK_ABI (verifies ebx/esi/edi across every direct call - found this chain in ONE run); find_reg_clobbers.py; dump_table.py. ALSO FIXED A MEASUREMENT BUG: triage_crash.py's load_map() stopped at 'entry point at' and never read MSVC's Static symbols section, loading 30,582 of 55,789 symbols - so every backtrace silently attributed addresses to the nearest LOADED symbol with a plausible-looking offset. It reported sub_001A016A+0x1CB for a function 0x60 bytes long. Every backtrace-based conclusion before this fix is suspect.

message: Seeded 1,049 unresolved stubs - the empty bodies were swallowing register restores and stack purges
note: Follow-on from the sub_001A0189 root cause. recomp_stubs_unresolved.c defined 3,205 addresses as EMPTY bodies, and all 3,204 that remain are actually called. In this calling convention the call site pushes a fake return address that the callee must pop, so an empty stub pops nothing and leaks 4 bytes of simulated stack per call, plus whatever argument purge the real function owed. 928 of them are reached by a lifter TAIL call, which is worse: they terminate a fragment chain, so the PUSH32/POP32 pairs that restore ebx/esi/edi across the chain never complete and the caller silently continues with someone else's registers. Confirmed on sub_001183A0 -> sub_001183C0 -> sub_001183ED, where the stub held the actual 'pop edi; pop esi'. Seeded 1,049 (908 tail-called + 121 new call targets the seeded bodies introduced + closure rounds); 9 have no findable terminating ret and now at least pop the return address. RESULT 52 -> 56 kernel calls, but failed icalls 1 -> 3 and safe-stub 1 -> 5. NOT treating the rises as a regression: 1,049 functions that previously did nothing now execute real code and make real indirect calls, so more of them can fail - the same 'two different programs' reading as the 200 -> 82 step. Verified the ABI checker is behaviour-neutral by rebuilding with it OFF: identical 56/3/2/5. BLOCKER UNCHANGED: esp goes NEGATIVE (0xFFFFFF80) in sub_002235D0, reached via sub_002221E0 <- sub_00209650 <- sub_002226E0. RECOMP_CHECK_ABI's esp guard reported nothing, so esp is not escaping across a direct call - it is going wrong inside a function or across an indirect call, which RECOMP_ABI_CALL does not wrap. That is the next thing to instrument. TOOL FIXES: seed_missing_functions.py overwrote recomp_seed.c each run, silently discarding the previous round - and because the addresses were already recorded as known starts, re-running did NOT restore them (908 functions became 121). It now carries forward existing bodies. stub_overridden.py could not see the one-line stub form and treated recomp_seed.c as a target rather than a source. Added normalise_seed_names.py: the seeder emits XbSymbolDatabase names for call targets while the main generation emits sub_ADDRESS, so 21 references failed to link.

message: Blocker fully characterised: infinite recursion in Alchemy's igMetaObject bootstrap
note: The negative esp is not a leak - it is unbounded recursion. Added an esp guard inside PUSH32 itself under RECOMP_CHECK_ABI (RECOMP_ABI_CALL only sees call boundaries, and this escapes inside a function), which named the exact push and showed a repeating 4-function cycle: sub_002235D0 -> sub_002226E0 -> sub_00209650 -> sub_002221E0 -> sub_002235D0. Each lap allocates 0x108 bytes, so esp walks the full 8 MB stack in roughly 33,000 laps and then leaves it. This is Intrinsic Alchemy, the engine the game is built on (see game/alchemy.ini): the strings involved are 'igMetaObject' at 0x3F9734 and 'igMetaObject: ' at 0x3F9860, so this is metaclass registration, and registering the ROOT metaclass is a bootstrap that has to break its own cycle. Ghidra gives the breaker exactly: FUN_002226e0 is 'if (*DAT_005bc508 != 0) { FUN_00209650(&LAB_002221e0); ... }' - the recursive registration path runs only when that byte is NON-zero; when it is zero the function takes FUN_001f7e00 and allocates directly, no recursion. So the guard is inverted in effect for us. Measured: MEM32(0x5BC508) = 0x00F81288, a heap object whose first dword is the vtable pointer 0x003F4770, so the byte read is 0x70 and the recursive path is always taken. 0x005BC508 lives in BSS and is 0x00000000 at load - confirmed with a write-watch, which armed on the value 0. So something sets it to a live object before igMetaObject itself is registered, and the bootstrap then eats itself. Not yet found WHAT sets it: the page-granular watch fired first on a neighbouring write to 0x005BC548 from sub_00011E40+0x1A1. Next step is a byte-exact watch on 0x5BC508, or working out which of the 357 callers of sub_002226E0 legitimately runs before the metaobject system is up. Signals unchanged at 56/3/2/5, deterministic, same crash site - this entry is analysis, not a fix.

message: Recursion traced to our own heap: xbox_HeapAlloc overwrites the core engine buffer
note: Made the write-watch byte-exact first. It was disarming on the first write anywhere in the 4 KB page, so a neighbour answered a question that was never asked - that is why the earlier attempt reported 0x5BC548 instead of 0x5BC508. It now steps the neighbouring write over with the trap flag, re-protects on the single-step, and keeps waiting; it also prints a backtrace and how many writes it stepped past. It needed 648 of them to reach the right one. CHAIN, ALL MEASURED: FUN_002226e0 takes the recursive igMetaObject registration path when the byte at *DAT_005bc508 is non-zero, and the direct-allocation path when it is zero. DAT_005bc508 is written exactly once, by 0x00239E50 - Ghidra names it alloc_core_engine_buffer - during a C++ static constructor under __cinit. That write is legitimate. The pointer lands on heap block 0x00F81288, and the watch confirmed that block was 0x00000000 when armed, which is the value the guard needs. The first write to it then came from xbox_HeapAlloc+0x94 (via bridge_NtAllocateVirtualMemory), NOT from game code - it wrote 0x003F4770, a .rdata vtable pointer. So OUR heap wrote into a block the game already owns: either it handed the same memory out twice, or its bookkeeping lives inside the region it returns. The game then reads a non-zero byte, believes the metaobject system is up before igMetaObject itself is registered, and the bootstrap eats itself - 33,000 laps of sub_002235D0 -> sub_002226E0 -> sub_00209650 -> sub_002221E0 until esp leaves the 8 MB stack. This is a bug in src/kernel, not in the lifted code, which is a much better place for it to be. Signals unchanged at 56/3/2/5 - analysis, not a fix.

message: Recursion narrowed to static-initializer ORDER, not a lifter bug
note: CORRECTION FIRST: I briefly concluded the lifter had dropped the 'already registered' guard at 0x00223614. It has not. recomp_0016.c:21403 carries it faithfully - 'if (CMP_NE(MEM32(ebx), 0)) goto loc_00223698' - and my grep pattern was simply wrong. Verified against Ghidra instruction by instruction over 0x0022360D..0x00223620. No lifter defect here. WHAT THE CYCLE ACTUALLY IS: FUN_002235d0 caches its result - the guard reads *param_1 (param_1 = 0x5BC274) and skips the whole creation block when non-zero - but the store '*param_1 = FUN_002226e0(...)' happens AFTER that call returns. So on the first entry the slot is legitimately 0, it calls FUN_002226e0, and if that re-enters registration the guard cannot help: nothing has been stored yet. Hardware must therefore never re-enter, and FUN_002226e0 is where it is decided: '*DAT_005bc508 != 0' takes the registration path, zero takes plain allocation via FUN_001f7e00. So on hardware *DAT_005bc508 is ZERO at this moment. MEASURED IN OUR PORT: DAT_005bc508 = 0x00F81288 with first byte 0x70 - the low byte of vtable pointer 0x003F4770 - so a constructed object already sits there. DAT_005bc508 is written exactly once, by 0x00239E50 (Ghidra: alloc_core_engine_buffer), from a C++ static constructor under __cinit. Ruled out with a byte-exact watch: the heap block was 0x00000000 when armed, and both early writes to it were xbox_HeapAlloc's own memset zeroing a fresh block - correct behaviour, not corruption. So the earlier 'our heap overwrote the buffer' reading was WRONG and is retracted. LEADING HYPOTHESIS NOW: static-initializer ORDER. alloc_core_engine_buffer runs before the igMetaObject bootstrap in our port; on hardware it must run after. _initterm (sub_001A3554) walks three sources in this order - MEM32(0x47A044), then [0x44B0A8,0x44B0BC), then [0x44A590,0x44B0A4) - and that order, or the boundary between the tables, is the thing to check next. TOOL: the write-watch is now byte-exact. It used to disarm on the first write anywhere in the 4 KB page, which is how a neighbour at 0x5BC548 answered a question about 0x5BC508. It now steps neighbours over with the trap flag and re-protects on the single-step; it took 648 of those to reach the right write. Added an optional 4th field, VA:SIZE:LABEL:SKIP, to let N matching writes past - the first write to a fresh heap block is always the allocator zeroing it. Signals unchanged at 56/3/2/5 - analysis only.

message: ROOT CAUSE of the igMetaObject recursion: threads run inline, so startup re-enters itself
note: Chased the guard byte to the end and it is NOT the bug - every piece of it is legitimate. alloc_core_engine_buffer (0x00239E50) allocates a block, constructs an object in it via sub_002154F0 (byte-exact watch, skipping the allocator's own memset, named the vtable write at sub_002154F0+0xAA), and stores the pointer in DAT_005bc508. The object's first byte is then the low byte of vtable 0x003F4770, i.e. 0x70, and FUN_002226e0 reads exactly that byte to decide between registering a metaclass and allocating directly. Also verified the 'already registered' guard in FUN_002235d0 is lifted faithfully AND reads the correct stack slot: probed it, ebx = 0x005BC274 (the igMetaObject slot) with the expected 0x120 displacement, and the slot is 0 every pass because the store only happens after the recursive call returns. THE ACTUAL CAUSE IS ORDERING. alloc_core_engine_buffer runs BEFORE the metaclass bootstrap, so the bootstrap starts in a world that already looks initialised and eats itself. Both paths arrive through bridge_PsCreateSystemThreadEx -> sub_0019F196 -> sub_001A1C23, at DIFFERENT offsets in the same function (+0x245 and +0x16B), which looked like out-of-order execution until sub_001A1C23 turned out to be a hand-written override in recomp_manual.c whose own comment states it: the port runs PsCreateSystemThreadEx start routines SYNCHRONOUSLY (kernel_bridge.c ~line 241, 'Call the start routine synchronously through the recomp dispatch'), so a thread created during startup runs to completion INSIDE startup - 71 nested entries measured. Those two offsets are different nested invocations, not a reordering. So the port has no concurrency: every worker thread the engine spawns during init runs immediately and completely, in the middle of the initialisation it depends on. The igMetaObject recursion is a symptom. NEXT TARGET IS THE THREAD MODEL, not this guard. The existing comment's warning still stands - do NOT block re-entry into sub_001A1C23, that was tried and cost 200 -> 44 kernel calls - because with inline threads the re-entry IS how threads run. The fix is to stop running them inline, which removes the need for re-entry rather than blocking it. Signals unchanged at 56/3/2/5.

message: Recovered the tree after a botched stage-2 attempt; found gen/ is not reproducible from a commit
note: WHAT I BROKE: attempting per-thread SEH, I taught disasm.py to keep the fs: segment override and _fmt_mem to emit g_fs_base + X. It produced ZERO sites - Capstone's mem.segment is not populated the way I assumed - so the change achieved nothing. Worse, before regenerating I ran 'manual_edits.py extract', which swallowed the 1,049 seeded function bodies into the hand-edit store (139 entries -> 1042). The regeneration then could not place them and the tree stopped linking; a repair loop diverged (16 -> 18 -> 18 -> 14 unresolved). Backed up the broken gen/ and rebuilt from the commit. RECOVERY PATH THAT WORKED: git checkout of tracked sources to bee574d; restore the PRE-seed seeded_functions.json from 65de1fd^ (the seeder filters out addresses already recorded as known starts, so re-seeding against the post-seed file is a no-op - that is the trap); delete recomp_seed.c; full regeneration; the documented recipe; then seed_missing_functions.py --stubs --tail-only --apply plus closure rounds on whatever the linker still wants; one address (sub_0023BF80) has no terminating ret and takes a purging stub. FINDING WORTH MORE THAN THE FIX: the rebuilt tree measures 54/4/2/8 where the commit measured 56/3/2/5. Same sources, same recipe, different result - so gen/ is NOT deterministically reproducible from a commit. gen/ is gitignored, so a fresh clone cannot reproduce a recorded number, and every progress entry is only as trustworthy as the gen/ that produced it. The seeding is order-dependent: which stubs get seeded versus stubbed depends on what the linker happens to demand, and that depends on the previous round. Making this deterministic - seed the full tail-called set in one pass from a recorded list rather than iterating on linker errors - is now a prerequisite for trusting any A/B measurement. message: The 195 skipped addresses are NOT junk - retracting that
note: Regenerated with the cleaned seed list. 864 seeded instead of 1,059, exactly the 195 the new classifier rejects as mid-function or override. Result: the closure went from 8 unresolved to 80, and the build still would not link. Restored the baseline; 54/4/2/8 confirmed. CORRECTION TO THE PREVIOUS ENTRY: I called those 195 addresses 'junk' and '18% of the seed set that was never valid'. That was wrong. They are mid-function call targets - real code that something genuinely calls. The classifier is right that the SEEDER should not manufacture them (a seeded body starting mid-instruction-stream and ending at whatever ret it reaches is a fabrication), but refusing to seed them does not make the calls go away. They fall through to purging stubs instead, which is the original defect this whole thread started from: an empty stub swallows the PUSH32/POP32 pairs that restore ebx/esi/edi. So a fabricated body was apparently serving better than no body. WHERE THE FIX ACTUALLY BELONGS: the lifter. It already splits functions at branch targets into fragments; these 195 are targets where the split did not happen, so nothing defines them. The right change is to make the splitter cover them - then they are real fragments of their containing function, with correct entry state, and neither the seeder nor a stub is involved. Concretely, sub_0023BF80 should be emitted as a label inside sub_0023BEE0's translation and reachable as a fragment, not conjured as a standalone function. WHAT IS SOLID FROM THIS ROUND: seeding replay is deterministic and proven (two runs byte-identical); --from-list is idempotent; the classifier correctly identifies what the seeder must not fabricate, and its output is now the worklist for the lifter fix. message: FOUND IT: manual_edits.py places only 68 of 153 edits against the tree it was extracted from
note: Direct test of the round-trip hypothesis, no regeneration needed. Ran 'manual_edits.py apply --partial --force' against the LIVE 54/4/2/8 tree - the same tree the store was extracted from, so every anchor should match by construction. It placed 68/153. The store is not incomplete - it has 153 entries against ~60 in-tree markers plus 73 'moved to' stub replacements, which is proportionate. The defect is in APPLY, not in EXTRACT. message: RETRACTION: the 68/153 result does not mean 85 edits are lost
note: Correcting the previous entry, which recorded a wrong conclusion. I ran 'manual_edits.py apply' against the already-applied live tree, got 68/153, and called it proof that 85 hand fixes are silently dropped on every regeneration. That inference does not hold. READING THE TOOL PROPERLY: replace_line has an explicit 'already applied is success, not failure' branch. insert_before has one too, and it is POSITIONAL rather than a whole-file text search, with a comment explaining why - many guards are worded identically, so a text search would make every duplicate look already-applied and silently drop it. wrap locates by the whole enclosed run rather than the anchor line, for the same reason. This is careful, well-reasoned code and I mischaracterised it. WHAT 68/153 ACTUALLY SHOWS: applying to a tree that already carries the edits is not the round-trip test I claimed it was. The reported failures are 'anchor line not found in function', and the likely mechanism is narrow - _find_anchor disambiguates using preceding context, and once a block has been inserted the line before the anchor IS that block, so the context no longer matches and an edit that is correctly in place reports as failed. That is a reporting artefact of re-running, not evidence of loss. WHAT IS STILL TRUE AND STILL UNEXPLAINED: two unrelated changes both regenerated to exactly 32/13/3/8 against a 54/4/2/8 baseline. Something in the recipe does not restore the live tree. But manual_edits is no longer the identified culprit - it is back to being one candidate among several, alongside find_icall_esp_saves only re-fixing four named functions. THE TEST THAT WOULD ACTUALLY SETTLE IT, and which I have not run: regenerate to scratch, run the full recipe, then diff the result against the live tree function by function. The differences ARE the loss. Anything short of that diff is inference. Also worth noting: apply --force wrote a partial tree during the diagnostic and I had to roll back from a snapshot. That behaviour is deliberate and documented in the source - it preserves ~100 good guards rather than discarding a whole file - but it does mean the tool is destructive on a re-run, which is worth a guard. FOUR REAL BUGS FIXED ALONG THE WAY, all of which blocked the regeneration from even linking, and none of which were in CLAUDE.md's recipe:
(1) The recipe says "copy in" - copying only *.c leaves the OLD recomp_funcs.h beside new sources. Single symptom: one undeclared identifier (sub_001A1C97, C2065) out of recomp_dispatch.c. Reads exactly like a generator bug. Copy *.c AND *.h.
(2) PowerShell Copy-Item PRESERVES the source mtime, so copied files look older than the .obj files and ninja skips recompiling them. Symptom was 304 phantom LNK2019s from a half-old object set. Touch after copying - snapshot.py already does this for its own restores, for the same reason.
(3) recomp_seed.c is NOT regenerated and the recipe never rebuilds it. Stale seeds referenced functions the new tree no longer defines. `seed_missing_functions.py --from-list seed_list.json --apply` is the documented rebuild and was missing from the recipe entirely. It must run BEFORE stub_overridden.py, which strips generated bodies it believes recomp_seed.c provides - with a stale seed file it stripped 994 instead of 871.
(4) The seeder skipped 195 mid-function addresses as "the lifter should split, not the seeder". Correct diagnosis, wrong remedy: the lifter only promotes call targets that TRANSLATED code references, and it never sees seeded bodies, so those addresses were seeded by nobody, promoted by nobody, stubbed by nobody, and the link failed on them. They now become fragments running from the target to the OWNER's end - the same rule the lifter's own promotion uses, and knowable here because containing_function() has the owner. 0 skips, seed_list back to its full 1,060. Plus a closure pass: 42 call targets have no decodable body at all (no terminating ret, scan artefacts into data) and now get the generator's own stub body, `g_esp += 4`, which pops the fake return address rather than leaking it. Those stubs must be DECLARED in the forward-declaration block, not defined after the bodies - RECOMP_ABI_CALL(sub_X) creates an implicit `int sub_X()` at the call site and a later `void` definition collides (C2371 x42).
NEW LEAD, and it is a good one. The rebuilt tree crashes reading Xbox VA 0xBEEF0079 in sub_001E8E20+0x46C, faulting on MEM32(eax + 0x78) with eax = 0xBEEF0001. 0xBEEF0001 is not garbage - it is the FAKE THREAD HANDLE that bridge_PsCreateSystemThreadEx writes to its output pointer (kernel_bridge.c:241). So a thread handle is being dereferenced as an object vtable. That points straight at the documented root cause - PsCreateSystemThreadEx runs start routines synchronously - rather than at anything the lifter did. Backtrace: sub_001E8E20 <- sub_00236500 <- sub_00239E50 <- sub_00011E40 <- sub_001A1C23 <- sub_0019F196 <- sub_0019F22E <- sub_001A1C97.
STATE: the rebuilt tree is snapshotted as 20260805-143108-af693d0-32-14-3-8-REBUILT-tree-32-14-3-8-after-full-correc.tar.gz for further diffing. message: igMetaObject recursion mapped: bootstrap gate is a vtable-install ordering window, not a broken guard
note:
Mapped the igMetaObject recursion precisely. No fix yet, but the question is now scoped to a window of a few instructions instead of "infinite recursion somewhere in class registration". Every step below is measured, not inferred.
THE CYCLE, with RVAs resolved through triage_crash.symbolise rather than eyeballed:
  sub_002226E0+142 -> sub_00209650+276 -> sub_002221E0+281 -> sub_002235D0+1138 -> back
(Those offsets are NATIVE offsets into compiled C, which is far larger than the original x86. I briefly mistrusted the attribution because sub_002221E0 is only 0x33 bytes of x86 and the report said +0x119 - that was my error: the function spans 304 NATIVE bytes. Do not "correct" this again.)
WHAT EACH LINK IS:
- sub_002221E0 registers exactly one class, passing 11 args including the name at 0x3F9734, which reads "igMetaObject" - the ROOT metaclass - plus size 0x64 and ctor 0x219A10.
- sub_002235D0 is the registrar. At source line 21406-21409 it holds the guard: ebx = the ppMeta argument, and `if (MEM32(ebx) != 0) goto loc_00223698` skips the work. The guard is CORRECT and cannot help, because the slot is only written at line 21463, AFTER the recursive call at line 21459 returns. Textbook bootstrap chicken-and-egg.
- sub_002226E0 is the gate: `eax = MEM32(0x5BC508); if (MEM8(eax) == 0) tail-call sub_00222708()` else run the registration path. sub_00222708 is the BOOTSTRAP - it allocates 0x64 bytes (matching the size igMetaObject is registered with), installs a vtable, and returns, with NO recursion. So the gate firing is what terminates this on hardware.
MEASURED, probe at the guard: first entry has ebx = 0x005BC2FC (some other class) with contents 0; every entry after that has ebx = 0x005BC274 (igMetaObject's slot) with contents 0, forever. So registering ANY class needs igMetaObject, and registering igMetaObject needs itself.
THE LIFTER IS NOT AT FAULT HERE. I read the raw XBE bytes at 0x002226E0: A1 08 C5 5B 00 | 80 38 00 | 74 1E ... which is exactly `mov eax,[0x5BC508]; cmp byte [eax],0; je 0x222708`. gen/ matches instruction for instruction. Two of my own hypotheses died here and should not be re-run: (1) that MEM32(0x5BC508) was null and the byte read was hitting our fake TIB at guest VA 0 - it is not null, it is 0x00F81288; (2) that the lifter had dropped a displacement - it had not.
WHAT [0x5BC508] IS: a 928-byte (0x3A0) manager, allocated by sub_00239E50 via operator new, member-initialised by sub_002154F0 - which explicitly writes MEM8(this) = 0 - then published with `MEM32(0x5BC508) = eax`. A probe at the publication point measured byte0 = 0x00 and dword0 = 0x00000000. So the gate byte is genuinely ZERO at publication, exactly as the gate needs.
THE ACTUAL FINDING: by the time sub_002226E0 reads it, dword0 is 0x003F4770 - and reading that address in the XBE gives 0x001FBA80, 0x001FBB80, 0x001FBA80, 0x0015FDF0, ... all valid .text addresses. It is a VTABLE, installed at offset 0 after publication, and 0x70 is merely its low byte. So the gate can only fire in the WINDOW between publication and the vtable install, and our run reaches class registration after that window has closed.
That is the whole question now: sub_00239E50 publishes the manager and immediately calls sub_00236500(this=manager); somewhere inside, the vtable gets installed AND class registration gets triggered. On hardware the registration must happen BEFORE the vtable store; in our build it happens after. Candidate vtable-install sites are the `MEM32(eax|esi) = 0x3F4770` stores in recomp_0015.c:44605, 44654, 56804, recomp_0016.c:57963 and recomp_seed.c:68601, 72373 - find which one runs on this path and what sits between it and the registration.
Worth noting for whoever picks this up: the ordering is exactly the kind of thing the nine missing CRT static-init thunks were perturbing, and those were only fixed today, so re-measure rather than trusting any pre-2026-08-05 statement about init order.
Baseline unchanged and re-verified at 54/4/2/8 through the whole investigation; all probes stripped; gate green.

message: igMetaObject recursion broken - boot reaches the registration machinery; gate red on failed_icalls 4->7, not re-baselined
note:
BROKE THE igMetaObject RECURSION. The boot now runs INTO the class-registration machinery instead of eating its own stack. Two changes, one certainly right and one provisional, and the gate is RED - read the trade before keeping this.
CHANGE 1, provisional, sub_002226E0 (recomp_0016.c): the bootstrap gate now also fires when the root metaclass slot is empty - `if (MEM8(eax) == 0 || MEM32(0x5BC274) == 0)`. Rationale: MEM8(eax) is byte 0 of the manager at [0x5BC508], which is genuinely 0 at publication (probed: byte0=0x00) but holds 0x70 by the time this runs - the low byte of vtable 0x003F4770 installed at offset 0 afterwards. So the original gate only separates the two cases inside a window our startup ordering misses. MEM32(0x5BC274) is the slot the machinery itself needs; while it is 0 the machinery cannot work whatever the byte says, and sub_002235D0 fills it from this call's result, so the condition stops applying once the bootstrap it enables completes.

message: NULL critical section traced to an uninitialised guest heap - RtlCreateHeap is not implemented and six guards already paper over it
note:
Chased the NULL critical section and it led somewhere much better than expected: it is a symptom of the guest HEAP STRUCTURE never being constructed, and that single defect already has SIX hand-written guards papering over it in one function.
HOW: a conditional recomp_where in bridge_RtlEnterCriticalSection, firing only when cs_va == 0, gave identical caller paths every time - sub_001A0B0C <- sub_003437C7 <- sub_003437F3 (operator new). So the NULL lock is the heap's own lock, taken on every allocation. In sub_001A0B0C the lock is fetched as MEM32(esi + 0x580) and passed to ICALL MEM32(0x3C6C5C); esi is the heap object, so the lock pointer is 0 because the heap object is zeroed rather than initialised.
THE REAL DEFECT, and it is already documented six times over in sub_001A0B0C's own guard comments: "on real hardware an initialised-but-empty head points AT ITSELF, which the original CMP_EQ catches. In our build the head reads 0, because the code that should self-initialise it has not run (ebx is the base of a 1MB block from NtAllocateVirtualMemory, so the memory is merely zeroed)." The heap's 128 bucket list heads at heap+0x180 are supposed to be circular lists linked to themselves; ours are all zero. Six guards translate "head == 0" into "empty list" one site at a time, and the NULL lock at +0x580 is the seventh symptom of the same missing construction.
RtlCreateHeap IS NOT IMPLEMENTED ANYWHERE in src/kernel - the only occurrence of the name in the whole tree outside gen/ is a comment in recomp_manual.c. So nothing ever builds that structure; the game gets a 1 MB zeroed block from NtAllocateVirtualMemory and proceeds.
THIS IS THE NEXT TARGET, and it is a fix rather than another guard: construct the guest heap properly - self-link the 128 bucket heads at heap+0x180 (each 8 bytes, next and prev pointing at the head itself), populate the lock at +0x580, and set whatever else sub_001A0B0C reads (+0x1C, +0x30, +0x160 bitmap, +0x60 table). Doing it once should let all six existing guards be deleted, which is the sign it is the right level to fix at. Establish the layout from sub_001A0B0C's own reads plus the ctor path rather than guessing.

message: RETRACTION: the guest heap IS correctly constructed - the real anomaly is heap+0x580 being zeroed at runtime
note:
RETRACTING LAST TURN'S HEAP THEORY. I said the guest heap was never constructed and that RtlCreateHeap was missing. Both wrong, and I got the NULL critical section wrong twice on the way. Measured instead of reasoned this time.
WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE. RtlCreateHeap is not a kernel export at all - the Xbox CRT implements its own heap over NtAllocateVirtualMemory, and _heap_init (sub_001A23F3) calls it as sub_001A06E8. That function is present and complete: it self-links the bucket heads at heap+0x180 in a do-while at loc_001A0A3C (MEM32(eax)=eax; MEM32(eax+4)=eax; eax+=8), sets up the large-block head at +0x58/+0x5C, and stores the lock at +0x580.
A probe at sub_001A0B0C's entry confirms the heap is FINE:
  heap=0x00F81000 bucket0.next=0x00F81688 expect=0x00F81180 lock=0x00F81610
  heap=0x00F81000 bucket0.next=0x00F81180 expect=0x00F81180 lock=0x00F81610   <- self-linked, i.e. correctly empty
  heap=0x00F81000 bucket0.next=0x00F81310 expect=0x00F81180 lock=0x00F81610
Bucket 0 is self-linked when the list is empty and points at real in-heap blocks otherwise. That is exactly what an initialised NT-style heap looks like. So the six "the head reads 0 because the code that should self-initialise it has not run" guards in sub_001A0B0C are describing a state this build no longer reaches - they are very likely stale relics from before today's allocator fix. Worth testing by removing them once the boot is further along; do NOT trust their comments as a current description of the heap.
THE ONE REAL ANOMALY, and it is not what I claimed. The lock pointer at heap+0x580 is 0x00F81610 - a valid embedded critical section sitting just past the bucket array - for the first four allocations, and 0x00000000 on the fifth. It starts VALID and gets ZEROED. So the null critical section from last turn is neither "the heap was never built" (my first claim) nor "the game asked for an unserialised heap" (my second) - it is a field being overwritten at runtime. heap+0x580 is immediately after the 128 bucket heads end at 0x580, so an off-by-one bucket write, or a block whose bookkeeping runs one entry long, would land exactly there. That is a concrete corruption target with a fixed guest address, which makes it ideal for the run --watch instrument: watch 0x00F81580:4 and it names the writing instruction.
Also worth noting the arg analysis that misled me: _heap_init pushes six args and I read ebp+0x18 as the lock parameter and concluded the game passes 0. The observed 0x00F81610 says my offset mapping was wrong. Do not re-derive that by counting pushes; probe it.
Not bailing out: XapiBootToDash is still never called and there are no RtlRip/assert lines.
Signals unchanged and deterministic at 100/195/11/192 across every build this turn. All traces removed. Gate still red because it will not baseline a hung run.
